tagline: River crossings link old mill towns, farms and stone buildings
intro: The Mills Scenic Byway links river crossings and mill towns with rolling farmland, woods and stone walls. It follows local streets and NH 4 in Rollinsford, then NH 108 through Madbury, Durham and Newmarket, with a break in the byway through Dover. Its 2016 corridor management plan identifies scenic, natural, historic, cultural, archaeological and recreational qualities, with nineteenth-century textile mills as the common thread. White church steeples, mill buildings and riverfront parks punctuate the downtown districts.

The corridor plan grew from work begun in 2009 and resumed in 2011 and 2014. The four towns worked with the Strafford Regional Planning Commission to form a byway committee and hold public meetings. Their purpose was to balance promotion with protection of the corridor’s resources. The resulting plan was adopted in October 2016.

Start at the South Berwick boundary on Front Street in Rollinsford, continuing by Main Street and Roberts Road to NH 4. NH 108 connects the gap through Dover to the next byway segment in Madbury. Madbury brings undulating hills and farm country; houses from the late 1700s and early 1800s once belonged to some of the town’s largest dairy farms. Continue through Durham across the Oyster River, then through Newmarket beside the Lamprey, ending at the Newfields town line.

moments.title: Rollinsford
moments.text: On Front Street, the Salmon Falls mill complex occupies a site where an earlier woolen factory burned in 1834. Cotton manufacturing followed, and the Number 2 Mill, built in 1848, used a turbine instead of a waterwheel to power its machinery. The mill buildings are predominantly brick, with additions designed to match the existing structures. Beyond the mills, a section of NH 4 parallels the Newichawannock trail, a Native American roadway predating 1600 that Revolutionary War soldiers used between Maine, New Hampshire and Boston. The Salmon Falls Manufacturing Company stopped production in 1927. The mills now contain artists’ and artisans’ studios, including spaces for painting and furniture making.

moments.title: Durham
moments.text: At Durham’s Oyster River crossing, the Jenkins mill occupied the dam site in the mid-1800s. Decay and the weight of snow eventually brought it down, reportedly in about 1955. The historic district extends along NH 108 and Main Street, with the Oyster River running through it. This settlement developed into a shipbuilding center in the eighteenth century. South of the river, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century houses line Newmarket Street; the Durham Community Church, built in 1848–49, anchors the district’s Main Street section. The 2016 Mills Scenic Byway Corridor Management Plan recorded the mill foundation as remaining at the dam site.

moments.title: Newmarket
moments.text: Newmarket’s mills made an unusual choice of building material: granite rather than the brick used in the Waltham factories they followed. By 1832, three mills were operating with 13,824 spindles. Stone also appears in the town’s houses, churches and schools. Surviving mills line the Lamprey River along the eastern side of the historic district. Commercial buildings stand across Main Street from the mills, with residential buildings on the side streets. To keep the mills running through drought, the company built upstream dams and released stored water into the Lamprey as needed.
